one_liner: C++20 web framework with ASP.NET Core-style minimal APIs on Boost.Beast; mixed against an unnamed C# server, slower than Drogon.
what_it_does: Mach is a C++20 HTTP/1.1 API framework: AppBuilder/App with mapGet/mapPost minimal-API routes, controllers, dependency injection with per-request scopes, JSON request binding via MACH_DEFINE_JSON (nlohmann/json), declarative validation, middleware, CORS and CSRF, and a CLI (mach new/run) shipped as .msi and .deb packages. Handlers return Reply objects (ok, noContent, badRequest, ...). It is a new framework, not a drop-in for any existing C++ server API; its shape copies ASP.NET Core rather than Drogon or Crow.
how_it_is_fast: Nothing specific to Mach: it is a Boost.Beast coroutine session loop (C++20 awaitables) on one shared Boost.Asio io_context run by threadCount threads (default 4; the benchmark server uses std::thread::hardware_concurrency). Each request is adapted into two std::unordered_map<std::string,std::string> (lowercased headers and cookies), passes a DI scope and a middleware pipeline, and the response body is copied into a Beast response. Its own numbers plateau at about 277k to 292k req/s from 4 wrk threads up, which fits a single shared reactor (inference, not measured).
when_to_use: Teams coming from ASP.NET Core who want the same minimal-API, controller, DI and validation model in C++20 on Windows (MSVC) or Ubuntu (GCC).
Internal JSON APIs where about 250k req/s per box on loopback (Mach's own framework runs, 16 threads / 100 connections) is far above the real load.
Projects that want an installer and project CLI (mach new, mach run) rather than wiring Boost.Beast by hand.
when_not_to_use: When throughput is the reason to switch: in Mach's own result files Drogon is faster on all 42 wrk rows (1.53x to 7.60x; plain 16/100 1,072,586 vs 280,386 req/s), and the C# server wins every 1-thread, 2-thread and large-JSON row.
Handlers that block (database, file or RPC calls): handlers are synchronous and run on the shared I/O threads; asynchronous handlers are an open roadmap item (#88).
Uploads or large bodies: request bodies are capped at 1 MiB, headers at 16 KiB and targets at 8 KiB in BeastSession.cpp; configurable limits are open issue #92.
TLS, HTTP/2 or macOS: none appear in the library's source list; v1.0 supports only Windows/MSVC and Ubuntu/GCC.
Production use that needs a track record: 4 stars, 0 forks, version bumped to 1.0.0 on 2026-09-23 with no tagged GitHub release.

integration.form: static lib (CMake target Mach::Mach) plus a CLI; Windows .msi and Ubuntu .deb packages
integration.dependencies: Boost.Asio and Boost.Beast (FetchContent downloads the Boost 1.90.0 source tarball if Boost is not found), nlohmann_json 3.12, fmt 12.1, spdlog 1.17; Catch2 for tests
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 with <format> and coroutines, CMake 3.26; MSVC on Windows, GCC on Ubuntu (minimum versions not documented)
integration.platforms: Windows x64 (MSVC) and Ubuntu amd64 (GCC); others 'may be supported in future releases'
integration.thread_safety: AppOptions is documented as not thread-safe during configuration and read-only safe afterwards; handlers run concurrently on up to threadCount I/O threads sharing one io_context, so handler and service state must be thread-safe.

gotchas: Harness flaws in benchmarks/runner/request_runner.py, the script behind the C# and Drogon comparison files: one 30 s run per row with no warm-up, wrk and the server (hardware_concurrency threads) on the same loopback host with up to 16 wrk threads, and only Requests/sec and latency are parsed, so wrk's 'Non-2xx or 3xx responses' and 'Socket errors' lines are never recorded. The C# file is internally inconsistent: at 16 threads / 100 connections its large-JSON-binding route (307,173 req/s) runs 3.06x faster than its empty 204 route (100,291 req/s) with identical 81-byte responses, so the 20-of-42 C# 'wins' for Mach track run-to-run noise as much as the framework (derived from page data). The newer framework_runner.py does record errors, warm-up and 5-run medians, but covers Mach alone.

Comparison servers do not return the same response: bytes per response derived from Transfer/sec divided by Requests/sec are 86 for Mach, 81 for the C# server and 127 for Drogon on every route, so Drogon's handler sends a bigger reply than Mach's 204 and still wins; the C# and Drogon server sources, versions and build flags are not in the repo.

BeastSession::handle_request sets 'Content-Type: text/plain' on every response after copying the handler's headers (src/server/BeastSession.hpp), and content-type is not on the reserved list, so a handler's own Content-Type such as application/json is overwritten (read from code at HEAD, not run).

BeastListener::do_accept creates each socket on its own strand but co_spawns the session on the raw io_context; the strand executor it computes is unused, so with more than one thread the session coroutine is not serialised with beast::tcp_stream's timeout handler, which BeastSession::run's comment says requires a strand (latent race on request timeouts; inference from code, not observed).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Mach over Drogon, Crow or Oat++ only for its ASP.NET Core-style API (minimal APIs, controllers, DI, validation) and Windows/MSVC packaging; on speed, Drogon beats it on every row of Mach's own comparison files, and Crow and Oat++ carry independent the-benchmarker or TechEmpower-style results that Mach lacks.
verified_claims_summary: Mach claims no speedup; its repo holds wrk CSVs (7 thread/connection configs x 6 routes, loopback, 30 s, no hardware or compiler stated) where Mach's release build beats a C# server of unknown version on 20 of 42 rows (all at 4 or more wrk threads, up to 2.80x on the 204 route at 16/100) and loses all 1-thread, 2-thread and large-JSON rows, while Drogon is 1.53x to 7.60x faster on all 42 rows. Mach-only framework runs from 2026-09-24 (commit 5705b5a, 5 runs, 5 s warm-up, zero socket errors and non-2xx) give a median 273,576 to 277,064 req/s plaintext and about 243k to 252k req/s for model-binding and controller routes at 16 threads / 100 connections.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-09-27, version bumped to 1.0.0 on 2026-09-23, four open v1.1.0 roadmap issues) and MIT-licensed, but a very young project with 4 stars and 0 forks whose own benchmark files do not show it beating the C++ incumbent.
